title: Jess Cornelius - Breaking and Entering
transcript:
Jess Cornelius joined Simon Winkler in the Triple R studio on 3 August 2017, ahead of Teeth and Tongue's Greatest Hurts farewell shows and a US tour with Paul Kelly. She discusses writing under her own name, revisiting the band's catalogue and preparing to spend time in Los Angeles. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: You won't be in the country for much longer. You're heading to America, a trip you had planned, but you've announced this week that you'll be touring the US with Paul Kelly.

Jess: Yeah, that was kind of an amazing development. I went to the States in February with my manager just to get a feel for the place and play a few shows, then came back and got all the visa process stuff happening because I knew I wanted to spend some longer periods of time over there. Got all that sorted, which is quite a big undertaking. It's quite a big investment, in a way. I was planning on spending three or four months there for the rest of the year, just hanging out and doing co-writing with people, meeting people and playing a few shows. We booked a few shows in LA and New York, just little ones, and then this tour came up. Now five weeks of the trip will be on the tour, and that's going to be wild because, other than playing with Paul Kelly every night, which is going to be really fun, I get to go to all these places I haven't been. Michigan and Portland and Atlanta. It's so many places.

Simon: For listeners coming to your music more recently, you've been writing and playing for a while. There are four records as Teeth and Tongue, I believe, many of them RRR Albums of the Week, if not all of them. The project has alternately been a solo pursuit, but then there's been Marc, Damian, James and Jade working with you at various stages. You'll be saying farewell to Teeth and Tongue for a while with your upcoming shows, one tomorrow and another on the eighth at Old Bar. Why is Teeth and Tongue going on hiatus in its current form?

Jess: Yes. It's a tricky one. I certainly don't want to say this is the end of Teeth and Tongue. I hope it isn't. But I've got an EP coming out under my name later this year, and then I have another album that I want to put out after that under my name. It feels like it might be a while before we do a record together. Like you say, it did start as a solo project, and it's gone in and out of that. I've played solo under the name Teeth and Tongue, but it really did become a more collaborative project. Marc has been with me for three albums, Damian for two and James for one and a half, really. I want to make the best use of their skills. If I do another record with them, I think it will be maybe an instrumental krautrock record or something where I'm not writing all the songs. If I have this actual solo project that I'm doing now, I guess a lot of the songwriting-type songs will go towards that. The songs are written in a really different way, which is why I decided to go under my name and change tack a little bit. The new stuff is very solo. It's written to be played with just a guitar and voice at the moment. That's how I'll be performing, and that's how it's been recorded. There are almost no instruments on the new EP. It is very different, and I love the band that has developed with Teeth and Tongue. If we do any recorded stuff together, it'll be, I think, a real collaboration.

Simon: The songs you're writing for yourself sound like you're stripping back a little to create a more minimalist space. Would you say that?

Jess: It definitely is. I don't so much know if it manifests as a difference in the song, but certainly the process. I don't know if the type of song is different, but whenever I wrote for Teeth and Tongue, I used to use computers a lot in the writing process. It started off as a drum machine band. I could always hear, oh, this would be where the drums come in, and the bass line would do something like this. I'd write different parts for it. I had this idea about the production, and I'd demo them. I might start with the drums. It was a very different process. With this solo project, I really wanted it to be enough to just have a guitar and voice. It's so weird because for years and years, ten years, I really avoided doing that. I thought, it's not going to be enough. I hate that term singer-songwriter. I came around to that. I really appreciate incredible, dense, layered production, and I always will. But I guess I'm just going through this phase where it's just about the song and the lyrics, and I wanted it to be kind of undiluted, I guess.

Simon: Presenting songs in an essential form, you seem fascinated with pulling apart your existing catalogue and recreating it. You had a set at Longplay earlier in the year with acoustic versions of existing songs. I don't even think it was drums, but boxes as percussion and acoustic guitar.

Jess: We did have a floor tom, I think. And I think I mentioned boxes as a joke. I became sort of obsessed with this nylon-string guitar I'd been given, and that's what I wrote a lot of the new stuff on. That actually came about from doing these Hush shows at Parliament House for Melbourne Music Week. The premise was that no one in the audience could make any sound during your performance, so it gave you the chance to do all this other stuff. When you do have those kinds of limitations, you can't make any noise, or a lot of noise. Everything has to be quiet. You also get all this opportunity because you get so much more space to play with. I am interested in reworking songs. We love reworking other people's songs as a band as well. It's always great when you get asked to do a cover of something and you do it really differently. I think that's just fun for musicians. It's just a fun job to do.

Simon: We've called upon you to do that a few times at RRR over the years. The two farewell shows, tomorrow at the Gasometer and August eighth at Old Bar, are called Greatest Hurts, which seems to have a bittersweet quality. Is it bittersweet revisiting some of these songs?

Jess: It's actually been really fun revisiting the songs, but it has brought up quite a bit of stuff. A couple of the older songs we have played right through, but it's been interesting going back, relearning them, and with the band as well. Marc was probably there for most of them. James hadn't played any of them, really. Some of them, like 'Lightness' from Monobasic, no one had really been around for. It has sort of put me back in the space I was in when I was touring those records. I dug up old videos, this one of us at Falls Festival, things at Polyester when Polyester was in the city, we did a live performance in there. The saddest thing is the band. I'll miss the band a lot.

Simon: But as you say, it's a farewell, not goodbye.

Jess: Yeah, for a time.

Simon: This one is from your most recent record, Give Up on Your Health. Could you introduce 'When We Met'?

Jess: I was going to say this is a personal song, but they usually are, so that doesn't make much difference. This is a love song, essentially, and it's a bit of a weird love song. But I think it's probably the closest I've ever come to writing one.

Simon: The album was called Give Up on Your Health. Was it in some ways a reflection on the sacrifices made in the artistic process?

Jess: Yes, I think that's probably a good reading, although I don't want anyone to take that too seriously because it is a choice you make. I think Amanda Roff from Time For Dreams, who you played earlier, put a note up the other day saying, 'I nearly threw this record off the West Gate Bridge.' It can be a tough thing to go through to create an album, and then you're not sure if anybody's really going to want to hear it, or they might hear it and hate it. There are lots of sacrifices to your own mental health, and financially as well. But it's also such a great thing to be able to do. It's just the best thing, so I'm not really wanting to complain about that.

Simon: It is a matter of keeping perspective and a balance. In the lead-up to your departure, you've been establishing a social media presence around the Jess Cornelius musical project. From the evidence, you've been living quite healthily. Are you making yoghurt at home?

Jess: I was making my own yoghurt, yes. I had to stop because my culture started to get a bit useless. That happens, apparently. I have to pick that up again, but things are getting a bit crazy with leaving, so I don't quite have time to nurture these. But I was very impressed with myself. It's a very soothing thing. When I was in Iceland, I was making sourdough bread, making the cultures and everything. I think there's this thing about growing things that ferment. It's a thing I like.

Simon: They are life themselves, so there's a companionship and nurturing element. That pre-empts my next question. The last time you were overseas for an extended period was in Iceland for an artist residency, working on material. You'd initially planned this America trip before the news of the Paul Kelly tour. What are your plans around writing, recording and working with other people while you're there?

Jess: It has certainly changed because of the tour, which is sitting right in the middle of it. Now I'll just have three weeks in LA. This is the craziest turn of events. The writer Chris Kraus, who wrote I Love Dick, she's got this TV series being made by Amazon at the moment. I put a post up on one of those closed Facebook housing groups saying I needed a three-week sublet. The only person who replied was Chris Kraus. Never met this woman. She's like, 'You can come and rent my house. My friend's staying in the guest house at the back.' I'm like, cool. I left it a bit late. It was getting down to the wire, really, and I didn't have anywhere to live. I'm going to be in her place, which I'm sure has a great library. I do have to do a bit of recording for a friend who's getting married. I'm going to record a song for her and hopefully make a video. I don't know how I'm going to get that done. I'm hoping I just meet someone who can make a video for the next single. I've got a few people I want to do some co-writing with, a few contacts there. I don't have any close friends there, but there's people like Shags and Romy from Macromantics. There's people there from Australia and obviously some Americans as well. It would be great to hang out with people who aren't just Australian. But I don't know. Now I've only got three weeks. I've got one show, then I'll go to New York for ten days and do three shows. They're all just my own little weird club shows or whatever. After the tour, when I come back to LA, I'm hoping I get a little bit more involved in the community.

Simon: Whenever Lauren and I chat with musicians and artists based in Los Angeles, I think they've all met Shags, and he's given them all the best impression of Melbourne musicians. I think he's become something of an ambassador. Romy's been based there for quite some time and has an incredible network of friends, so I'm sure it'll be a fruitful time to collaborate. Chris Kraus maybe can involve you in her projects as well.

Jess: That's it. Maybe I'll meet Kevin Bacon.

Simon: We're wishing you the very best for your time over there. I hope it's productive and enjoyable. For anyone who missed it, tomorrow, August fourth at the Gasometer, and August eighth at Old Bar with Loose Tooth, Gregor and Venetian Blinds DJs. But the tickets are all sold out, is that right?

Jess: Yeah, both shows are sold out, which is a real bummer. But I'm sure we will do it again at some point.

Simon: We look forward to that very much. Thanks again, Jess.

Jess: Thanks, Simon.
